title: Intermolecular forces
examples: What is the strongest intermolecular force?
How does the type of bond affect boiling point?
Can you compare the forces in water versus methane?

explain.say: Today we will explore forces between molecules. These are called intermolecular forces. They are weaker than bonds inside a molecule.
The first type is London dispersion forces. These exist between all molecules. They arise from temporary shifts in electron density.
Next we look at dipole-dipole forces. These occur between molecules with permanent dipoles. One end is slightly positive, and the other is slightly negative.
Hydrogen bonding is the strongest of these three. It happens when hydrogen is bonded to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine. Water is a classic example.

draw.text: H-Bonding: H bonded to N, O, or F

explain.say: These forces determine the boiling point. Stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to overcome. Therefore, they result in higher boiling points.
Consider comparing methane and water. Methane has only weak London forces. Water has strong hydrogen bonds, giving it a much higher boiling point.

faq.q: Do all molecules have London dispersion forces?
faq.a: Yes, every molecule has London dispersion forces. These forces are always present due to the movement of electrons.
asks: Does every molecule have these forces?

faq.q: Is hydrogen bonding only for water?
faq.a: No, hydrogen bonding can occur with other molecules. It requires hydrogen to be directly attached to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine.
asks: What atoms are needed for H-bonding?

faq.q: Which force is the strongest overall?
faq.a: In general, hydrogen bonding is the strongest of the three types discussed. However, molecular size also plays a role.
asks: Does size matter for force strength?

faq.q: Why does boiling point change with forces?
faq.a: Boiling requires enough energy to separate molecules from each other. Stronger forces mean more energy is needed to break them apart.
asks: How does force relate to boiling?

faq.q: Are dipole-dipole forces only in polar molecules?
faq.a: Yes, dipole-dipole forces exist between polar molecules. A polar molecule has a permanent separation of charge.
asks: Do non-polar molecules have this force?

facts: London dispersion forces increase with increasing molecular size.
Hydrogen bonding is significant when H is bonded to N, O, or F.
Stronger intermolecular forces lead to higher boiling points.
Dipole-dipole forces occur between permanent dipoles.
